phonemes.desc: A voiced aspirated 'b' — 'b' released with a breath of air — followed by the diphthong 'ai' as in English 'eye'.
The retroflex 'ṣ': the tongue curled back, as for the vowel in 'try'; then a short open 'a'.
A soft 'j' as in 'juice' running into the glide 'y' as in 'yes' — the three letters packed into one quick syllable.
Hard 'g' as in 'go', a short 'u' as in 'put', and the final syllable '-ru' lightly lengthened: GU-ru.

pronunciation.approximation: 'BY-shaj-yah-GOO-roo' — the 'sh' is retroflex, tongue curled back; the first syllable is aspirated and the last is lengthened.

kin.label: Indo-Iranian root
kin.form: bhaiṣajya 'medicine, healing' from bhiṣaj 'healer' — cognate with Avestan baēšaza- 'healing, cure' (the Zoroastrian term baēšazaŋh-), from Indo-Iranian *bhaiš-.

kin.label: Indo-European root
kin.form: guru 'heavy, weighty; venerable teacher' — cognate with Greek βαρύς (barús) 'heavy', Latin gravis, and English 'grave' (PIE *gʷerh₂-).

kin.label: Name-form
kin.form: Yàoshī Rúlái 藥師如來 — the Chinese 'Medicine Master Thus-Come-One,' the form the name took across East Asia.

pronunciation.note: Bhaiṣajyaguru is Tier 1 by the mechanical rule: the retroflex ṣ and the conjunct -jy- carry diacritics and script features the ASCII 'bhaisajyaguru' flattens beyond recognition. The full Sanskrit title is Bhaiṣajyaguruvaidūryaprabhārāja, 'Medicine Master, King of Lapis-Lazuli Radiance' (IAST).

domains.title: Healing
domains.subtitle: Healing, Medicine, Lapis-Lazuli Light
domains.lead: Bhaiṣajyaguru is the Buddha of medicine — the Medicine Master whose eastern paradise glows with lapis-lazuli light and whose twelve great vows promise healing not only for the sick but for the poor, the imprisoned, and the misled. In a Buddhist cosmos crowded with transcendent realms, his is the one built like a hospital.

cards.name: Healing
cards.desc: The central domain: his twelve vows promise to cure disease and deformity — and the poverty that makes sickness fatal.

cards.name: Medicine master
cards.desc: The name means "Medicine Master" — guru of bhaiṣajya, the healer's art, from bhiṣaj "healer."

cards.name: Unicode Restoration
cards.desc: The restoration Bhaiṣajyaguru recovers what plain ASCII bhaisajyaguru flattens.

cards.name: Original Attestation
cards.desc: Attested in Sanskrit manuscripts in Devanāgarī as भैषज्यगुरु; carried to China as Yàoshī, to Japan as Yakushi.

symbols.name: Lapis-lazuli light
symbols.meaning: The radiance of his eastern paradise — in his second vow, his very body is to shine like vaidūrya, the blue stone that gives him his title.

symbols.name: The medicine bowl
symbols.meaning: Held in his left hand, it carries the myrobalan (harītakī) — the one attribute no other major buddha needs.

symbols.name: The myrobalan fruit
symbols.meaning: The healing berry he offers, called in Ayurveda 'the remover of disease' — medicine as a concrete object, not a metaphor.

symbols.name: The eastern direction
symbols.meaning: His pure land lies in the east, balancing Amitābha's western paradise — dawn against sunset.

symbols.name: Sun and moon radiance
symbols.meaning: The bodhisattvas Sūryaprabha and Candraprabha attend him — light and its reflection as healing's witnesses.

mythology.lead: The stories of Bhaiṣajyaguru are sutras, not epics: scripture built from his twelve vows, his lapis-lit eastern paradise, and the liturgy of healing his name still powers across Asia.

myths.title: What He Promised Before He Was Buddha
myths.text:
The Bhaiṣajyaguruvaidūryaprabhārājasūtra — in Xuanzang's Chinese translation of 650 CE (T. 450), the standard form in East Asia — first tells what the future Medicine Buddha swore as a bodhisattva: twelve vows. He would make his body shine like lapis lazuli to dispel the darkness of ignorance; he would give beings 'inexhaustible' wealth of goods; he would set those on false paths on the bodhisattva road; he would restore broken precepts and heal 'bodies incomplete' — the blind, the lame, the deaf; he would cure the destitute sick and free the imprisoned from their chains; he would feed the hungry and clothe the naked. One vow — that women who wish it be reborn as men — belongs to its century, and modern translators note it without flinching.

The list is the myth: a buddha defined entirely by his promises, and a definition of healing broad enough to include poverty, fear, and error along with disease.

myths.title: The World of Lapis Light
myths.text:
Having fulfilled the vows, Bhaiṣajyaguru presides over the eastern pure land the sutras call Vaidūryanirbhāsa — 'Pure Lapis-Lazuli Radiance'. Its ground is vaidūrya itself, transparent as glass; its avenues are bounded by cords of jewels; streams run through it sounding the teaching, and music plays without any musician touching an instrument — Yijing's longer translation of 707 (T. 451) spells the geography out in loving detail. There is no trace of the lower destinies — no hells, no hungry ghosts, no animal births — and beings in difficulty who hear his name and remember it are, the sutra promises, rescued at the moment of death. Devotees who wish it may also choose rebirth in Amitābha's western paradise; the two buddhas are colleagues, not rivals.

If Amitābha's west is the sunset of this life's grief, Bhaiṣajyaguru's east is its remedy: a paradise designed like a hospital, staffed like a pharmacy.

myths.title: How the Medicine Master Crossed Asia
myths.text:
The cult rode translation. Xuanzang brought the shorter Sutra of the Merit of the Original Vows of Bhaiṣajyaguru back from India and rendered it in 650, fixing the Chinese name Yàoshī Liúlíguāng Rúlái — 'Medicine Master, Lapis-Lazuli Light, Thus-Come-One.' A generation later, in 707, the pilgrim Yijing translated a longer sibling text (T. 451), the Sutra of the Seven Medicine Buddhas, which surrounds Bhaiṣajyaguru with six other healing buddhas and preserves his healing dhāraṇī — a string of Sanskrit syllables still recited over the sick in Tibetan, Chinese, and Japanese monasteries. From China the sutra passed to Korea and, by the early seventh century, to Japan, where the Medicine Master's name contracted to the two syllables every Japanese still knows: Yakushi.

A name's journey is the tradition's own map: Sanskrit to Chinese to Japanese in three generations, with the pharmacy intact at every border.

myths.title: Two Lights and Twelve Generals
myths.text:
Bhaiṣajyaguru never travels alone. The triad tradition gives him two bodhisattvas — Sūryaprabha, 'Solar Radiance,' and Candraprabha, 'Lunar Radiance' (Nikkō and Gakkō in Japan) — the sun and moon standing at a healer's shoulders. Below them serve twelve yakṣa generals, each commanding seven thousand spirit troops, who swore before the Buddha to protect anyone who keeps the sutra: Kumbhīra, Vajra, Mihira, and nine more, their rolls recited in the liturgy to this day. Iconography fixed the ensemble early: the Medicine Buddha sits in monk's robes, his right hand in the gesture of gift-giving or holding a sprig of myrobalan, his left cradling the medicine bowl — the only major buddha whose standard attribute is a drug.

Solar light, lunar light, and a dozen bodyguards: the myth's arithmetic says healing is never a private act — it comes escorted, lit, and guarded.

lore.syncretism: Every Buddhist culture adopted the Medicine Master and filed him differently. In China he heads the 'Three Saints of the East' with Sūryaprabha and Candraprabha, and his sutra joined the scriptures chanted for the dead and the dying in the standard funerary liturgy alongside the Amitābha and Avalokiteśvara texts. Japan made him one of the most-culted buddhas of all: Emperor Tenmu vowed a temple to Yakushi for his ailing empress in 680 — the temple is Nara's Yakushi-ji — and esoteric Buddhism paired him with Amida as healer of body and soul. Tibet received him as one of the Eight Medicine Buddhas, invoked against illness through the dhāraṇī Yijing translated. Korean Buddhism chants his name in the Yaksa-je rite still held for the sick. Across all of it, the constant is concrete: medicine for the body first, metaphysics second.
lore.culturalLegacy: Yakushi-ji in Nara — UNESCO-listed, its East Pagoda a surviving seventh-century original — is his most famous monument, and the temple's Hossō-school triad became the template for a thousand Japanese healers' images; Shin Yakushi-ji, also in Nara, preserves the finest set of the twelve generals in clay, a designated National Treasure. In the modern West, 'the Medicine Buddha' has become a familiar presence: Birnbaum's The Healing Buddha (1979) introduced his cult to English readers, his image hangs in hospitals and hospices, and the dhāraṇī is chanted in meditation centers from Kyoto to California. The myrobalan in his bowl — harītakī, the 'remover of disease' — is still stocked in Ayurvedic pharmacies. His oldest promise, that no one should die for want of medicine, reads now like a plank of public health policy.
lore.extendedMeditation:
Bhaiṣajyaguru is the answer to a question most religions dodge: does the sacred care about bodies? His twelve vows say yes, at length — and not only about the dramatic body in crisis but about the poor body, the imprisoned body, the body that goes cold for want of clothing. Healing, in his charter, is social or it is nothing: you cannot cure a fever in a person who will starve tomorrow.

What he models is a vow as a technology — the bodhisattva who looked at the world's suffering, itemized it, and swore an itemized remedy. It is an oddly modern figure: the physician as bodhisattva, the hospital as pure land, medicine as a form of compassion you can measure. When modern health systems debate whether care is a right or a market, the Medicine Master sits at the corner of the debate, bowl in hand, having answered long ago.
lore.archaeology: The iconographic record is rich and datable. Dunhuang's Mogao caves preserve Tang-dynasty wall paintings of the Bhaiṣajyaguru paradise — lapis ground, jewel cords, celestial musicians — among the most complete sutra illustrations surviving. In bronze, gilt-copper Yakushi triads of the Asuka and Hakuho periods mark the cult's arrival in Japan; the Yakushi-ji founding of 680 under Emperor Tenmu is documented in the Nihon Shoki, and the temple's excavated foundations and surviving East Pagoda anchor the tradition in seventh-century fact. Shin Yakushi-ji in Nara preserves its eighth-century Twelve Generals in near-original clay — the single most important sculptural set of the cult. Dedicatory inscriptions across northern China and the Korean peninsula record the sutra's recitation for named donors, giving the healing cult thousands of individual faces.

lore.originalScriptNote: Written in Devanāgarī as भैषज्यगुरु: bhaiṣajyaguru joins bhaiṣajya, 'medicine, healing' (from bhiṣaj, 'healer'), to guru, 'master, venerable teacher.' The retroflex ṣ — tongue-tip curled back — is a phoneme English lacks entirely, and the conjunct -jya- packs three letters into one syllable. Xuanzang rendered the full title 藥師琉璃光如來, 'Medicine Master, Lapis-Lazuli Light, Thus-Come-One'; Japanese monks compressed it to the two syllables Yakushi.
